newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian duty-free chain sees growth potential.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian duty-free chain sees growth potential.

text.p: The increasing number of tourists visiting Indonesia is a boon for the country's largest duty-free operator, PT Sona Topas Tourism Industry, which expects earnings at its duty-free chain to grow in tandem.

"With technical assistance from U.S.-based Duty Free Shoppers (DFS) and a sustained rising number of tourist arrivals, it should not be a problem to achieve strong earnings growth in the coming years," president director Djoni Lasmana told Reuters on Friday.
Lasmana said the company expected its core business -- duty-free shopping -- to boost net profit to 25 billion rupiah ($10.3 million) in 1997 from 13.6 billion rupiah in 1996.
Sona's ticketing and travel services business was seen remaining insignificant in terms of revenues due to stiff competition and lower net profit margins, he said.

"Around five million tourists visited the country last year, some 1.1 million of them going to Bali. Many of them came from Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, who traditionally are among the best shoppers," Lasmana said.

Bail is important for the company because earlier this year it opened its latest duty free shop on the resort island. The shop has a selling space of 8,000 square metres, which boosted the firm's total selling space to some 12,000 square metres.
"Our new duty free shop in Bali is the largest in the world, I think. It should help our duty free business in the island to remain a major contributor to total earnings," Lasmana said.
He added Sona expected Indonesia to attract a total of 5.5 million tourists this year, with some 1.3 million of them visiting Bali.
Indonesia earned some $6 billion from tourism in 1996, up 18 percent from 1995, making the sector among the country's largest foreign exchange earners.
Given Indonesia's more than 16,000 islands and wide cultural diversity, opportunities for future growth in tourism were huge when the needed infrastructure was in place, Lasmana said.

He said the firm has already captured about a 60 percent share in the country's duty free shopping industry and that it has outlets in all of Indonesia's major tourist areas, including Bali, Bintan Island near Singapore, and Jakarta.
Lasmana said duty free shopping would remain an inseparable part of the tourism industry and that it offers higher net profit margins than other types of retail businesses.
Sona's strategic alliance with DFS, formed in the early 1990s, should help the firm to compete with other companies in the sector including several new entrants, he said.

DFS, the largest duty-free shopping network in the world, with more than 200 outlets in 14 countries, guarantees world-wide after-sales service of Sona's products and offers buy backs of idle inventory, Lasmana said.

"The worldwide guarantees and the buy backs, also the fact that most of our customers are tourists from some rich Asian countries, enabled us to achieve a strong gross profit margin of almost 50 percent last year."
Lasmana said DFS guaranteed that gross margins on Sona's imported goods would not be lower than 47 percent.
Sona sourced some 90 percent of its products from DFS, while the remainder was sourced from local companies, he said. ($1=2,435 rupiah)
